$6,900 MISHAP
Tony Bettenhausen, Tinley Park, Ill., was
on his way to victory and a purse of more
than $9,000 to the winner in the August 28,
1960, 200 mile big car race here. At 176 miles
the Lindsey Hopkins Spl. he was driving
started to act up. The universal joint became
overheated, setting fire to the upholstery.
Tony sat on the tail of the car, guiding it to.
the pits at 182 miles. He saw going up in
smoke more than $6,900, the difference be-
tween first and 14th places.
AL KRAUSE PHOTO
BOB CLEBERG SPIN
Fighting for a starting spot in
the 100 miler, a field of 20 cars
hit the first turn in the 20 mile
added event here June 5, 1960.
Bob Cleberg, formerly of Rio,
Wis., now of Phoenix, Ariz., spun
and scattered the last four rows
of cars. No one hurt, no cars
damaged. On the restart, Eddie
Sachs, Center Valley, Pa. (No. 6-
Dean Van Lines Spl.) won the
race, followed by Dick Rath-
mann, Roselle, Ill. (No. 45-Braund
Plywood Spl.).
RUSS LAKE PHOTO
FREE RIDE FOR RODEE
Chuck Rodee, veteran Indianapolis driver,
clipped the north turn wall after a spin on
the 23rd mile of the August 28, 1960, 200 miler
here. The emergency jeep, first to reach
Rodee tied a line on the Dunn Engineering
Spl. and gave him a free ride back to the pits.
After an official inspection, Rodee was al-
lowed to continue in the race, but to no
avail. Rodee's car wasn't running right and
he was given the red flag with only 166 miles
to his credit.
ARMY KRUEGER PHOTO

RACING IN REVERSE
On the 18th mile of the June 5, 1960 Rex Mays race here, Jim Hurtubise, Lennox, Calif. (No. 56-Travelon
Trailer Spl.) spun going into the north turn. Right behind came Don Branson, Champaign, Ill. (No. 7-Bob
Estes Spl.). Branson also spun to avoid the Hurtubise car. The ironic part was that Hurtubise kept his car
running and continued in the race. Branson's mount stalled and he was through for the day.

While he had raced around the coun-
try at hundreds of tracks, Tony always
had a warm spot for Milwaukee in his
heart. He constantly referred to Mil-
waukee as "his home away from home."
In an interview last year, he remarked,
I probably know more people in Mil-
waukee than in Tinley Park or Chicago.
I like the track and I like the fans.'
Tony proved this time and time again.
Worn out from a tough race, he never
turned down the request for an auto-
graph. After winning a race he would
find a comfortable seat in the infield,
kick off his shoes, have a cool drink,
light a cigarette, and call out to the
officials that he was ready too sign
autographs.
TONY LIKED SPRINT CARS TOO
HARRY GOODE PHOTO
Tony first came into prominence in Milwaukee when he won the 1942 outdoor midget championship on
the one-quarter mile dirt track. He came back to win the midget car titles here again in 1946 and 1947. His first
national championship victory at Milwaukee was in the June 11, 1950, 100 mile speedway big car race, which
was the first of the Rex Mays Classics. He came back to win the race again in 195i here. It is likely that if Tony
had moved to Milwaukee at this time, he could have run for mayor and rolled into office in a landslide vote.
The 1951 season was perhaps the greatest of Tony's career and certainly the greatest performance in one
season by any driver in racing. He won eight of 13 national championship races in the now-famous Murrell
Belanger blue-black No. 99. Earning nearly 2,400 points that season, Bettenhausen won the title in a walk.
Although he was heading for the 45 mark, Tony proved last summer that he had lost none of his consumate skill.
He won two late model stock car races and the 100 mile midget race as well. Since 1950 he won five stock car,
three midget, and two speedway big car races here. In 1959 and 1960, he was headed for victory in the 200 mile
big car grinds but in each case, mechanical trouble forced the gallant Dutchman to quit. And in each of these
races trouble struck with less than 30 miles to go.
Tony was a model family man as well. He farmed 600 acres at Tinley Park where he lived with his wife,
Valerie and four children: Gary 19; Merle, 17; Susan, 15, and Tony Lee, 9. He had remodelled the farm home
where he had lived all his life with his racing earnings and developed into a successful farmer-businessman.
His aptitude at learning new farming methods comes as no surprise to those who knew him. He became the best
among the race drivers and wanted only
the best for his family.
WINNING JULY, 1959, 150 MILE STOCK CAR RACE
ARMY KRUEGER PHOTO
Since 1950, Tony made many speak-
ing appearances here before church, high
school students, and fraternal groups.
He had an excellent memory and could
rerun every race when he got together
over cocktails or dinner with friends or
business acquaintances.
For those who read of Tony Betten-
hausen and his accomplishments at some
future date, he will serve as an inspira-
tion. Auto race director Tom Marchese,
grieved by the loss of his long-time
friend, remarked, "There'll never be
another like Tony. The Good Lord broke
the mold right after he created Tony."
Racing fans will miss him and his great
talent, and the fans at Milwaukee will
be especially lost without the appear-
ance of the "Tinley Park Express."
